units.name: Organic Chemistry
units.summary: Carbon compounds, and why carbon is special.

topics.name: Hydrocarbons
topics.summary: Alkanes and alkenes, and how to tell them apart.

objectives.text: Explain why carbon forms so many compounds.
Distinguish alkanes from alkenes by structure and formula.
Describe a test that tells them apart.

keyTerms.definition: A compound of hydrogen and carbon only.
A hydrocarbon with only single C–C bonds. Saturated.
A hydrocarbon with at least one C=C double bond. Unsaturated.
Holding as many hydrogen atoms as possible.

sections.heading: What you will learn
sections.body: Organic chemistry is the chemistry of carbon compounds, and there are millions of them. This lesson explains why carbon is unusual, and covers the two simplest families.

sections.heading: Why carbon
sections.body:
A carbon atom forms FOUR bonds, and — unusually — it bonds strongly to other carbon atoms.

That means carbon can build chains, branches and rings of almost any length, with hydrogen filling the remaining bonds.

No other element does this to nearly the same extent, which is why there are millions of carbon compounds and comparatively few of most other elements.

sections.heading: Alkanes
sections.body:
ALKANES have only SINGLE bonds between carbons. Every carbon holds as many hydrogens as it can, so they are SATURATED.

General formula: **CₙH₂ₙ₊₂**

    methane  CH₄     (n=1: 2×1+2 = 4) ✓
    ethane   C₂H₆    (n=2: 2×2+2 = 6) ✓
    propane  C₃H₈    (n=3: 2×3+2 = 8) ✓
    butane   C₄H₁₀   (n=4: 2×4+2 = 10) ✓

Names end in **-ane**. They are fairly unreactive, because a single C–C bond is strong and there is no room to add anything.

sections.heading: Alkenes
sections.body:
ALKENES have at least one DOUBLE bond between carbons (C=C). The double bond uses bonds that would otherwise hold hydrogen, so alkenes carry FEWER hydrogens — they are UNSATURATED.

General formula: **CₙH₂ₙ**

    ethene   C₂H₄    (n=2: 2×2 = 4) ✓
    propene  C₃H₆    (n=3: 2×3 = 6) ✓
    butene   C₄H₈    (n=4: 2×4 = 8) ✓

Names end in **-ene**. Compare directly:

    ethane C₂H₆  vs  ethene C₂H₄

Same two carbons, two fewer hydrogens, because one pair of bonds went into the C=C.

Alkenes are MORE reactive than alkanes. The double bond can open up and let other atoms add across it — which is exactly what the test below detects.
sections.example:
The bromine water test.

Bromine water is orange-brown. Shake a hydrocarbon with it:

    ALKANE  → stays orange-brown. No reaction.
    ALKENE  → turns COLOURLESS, quickly.

Why? The alkene's double bond opens and bromine adds across it, forming a colourless product. The alkane has no double bond to open, so nothing happens.

This is a genuinely useful test: a clear, immediate, visible difference from one property — unsaturation.

Exam wording matters here. "Decolourised" is the correct term, not "turns white" or "goes clear". The solution becomes colourless.

sections.heading: Try it yourself
sections.body:
1. Why can carbon form so many compounds?
2. Give the molecular formula of the alkane with 5 carbons, using CₙH₂ₙ₊₂.
3. C₃H₆ — alkane or alkene? How do you know from the formula alone?
4. Describe what you would see when bromine water is shaken with ethene, and with ethane.
5. Explain why an alkene is called unsaturated.

sections.heading: Summary
sections.body:
• Carbon forms four bonds and bonds to itself, so it builds chains and rings.
• Alkanes: single bonds only, saturated, CₙH₂ₙ₊₂, names end -ane.
• Alkenes: at least one C=C, unsaturated, CₙH₂ₙ, names end -ene.
• Alkenes are more reactive; the double bond can open and add atoms.
• Bromine water is decolourised by an alkene, unchanged by an alkane.

questions.question: C₃H₆ — is this an alkane or an alkene?
questions.explanation: Alkenes follow CₙH₂ₙ. With n = 3, 2n = 6, so C₃H₆ fits — it is propene. An alkane with 3 carbons would be CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ = C₃H₈. Test the formula against both patterns rather than guessing from the name.

questions.question: What happens when bromine water is shaken with an alkene?
questions.explanation: The C=C double bond opens and bromine adds across it, forming a colourless product, so the orange-brown colour disappears. An alkane has no double bond to open and leaves the colour unchanged. Use "decolourised" — not "turns white" or "goes clear".

questions.question: Why does carbon form so many different compounds?
options: It is the most common element
It forms four bonds and bonds strongly to other carbon atoms, building chains and rings
questions.explanation: Four bonds per atom plus strong carbon-to-carbon bonding lets carbon build chains, branches and rings of almost any size. Very few elements do this, which is why carbon compounds number in the millions while most elements form comparatively few.
